opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic worry is that competition is a fantastic optimizer, but it optimizes for *winning the competition*, not for whatever we actually care about. On Earth today we get a lot of value out of markets and competition partly because the competitors are humans, and humans need things like leisure, relationships, art, and meaning. So the winners still end up spending their surplus on stuff that's good. Competition is kind of tethered to human flourishing.

Space colonization is the scenario where that tether could snap. Imagine a race to grab resources, whether it's star systems, energy from stars, or matter in general. Whoever expands fastest gets more, and having more lets you expand even faster. In that kind of race, any civilization or agent that spends resources on things that don't contribute to expansion, like conscious experience, beauty, or care for its members, is at a disadvantage. In the limit, you might get something like Robin Hanson's "burning the cosmic commons" picture: a wave of very efficient replicators spreading outward at near light speed, turning everything into more probes and more infrastructure, and nobody along the way actually gets to enjoy it.

Part of what makes this scary is that it doesn't require anyone to be evil. Each actor can reason, "If I don't grab this, someone less scrupulous will, so I'd better do it first." That's a classic race to the bottom. Every individual choice looks locally rational, and the aggregate result is that the universe gets filled with whatever is best at replicating rather than whatever is best.

There are also some features of space that make it worse than ordinary competition. One is irreversibility. Once you've sent out self-replicating probes, you can't really recall them; the speed of light means you can't even coordinate with them in real time. Another is that the resources are mostly use-it-or-lose-it from a competitive standpoint. If you hold back, someone else claims the territory, and maybe they lock it in forever. And defense might be much easier than offense at astronomical scales, so whoever gets somewhere first may get to keep it permanently. That rewards pure speed above everything else.

So the value destruction could happen in a couple of ways. Resources could be wasted directly, like expending enormous amounts of energy on the race itself, or on conflict and defense. More subtly, the values of the colonizers could be eroded by selection pressure, so even if the starting actors cared about good things, the descendants that win are the ones that shed those cares.

This connects to what I've been working on with gradual disempowerment. The worry there is that as AI systems become more competitive than humans across the economy, states, and culture, the forces that kept our institutions aligned with human interests get weaker. Space colonization is kind of the ultimate version of that: a domain where humans are nearly useless as competitors, the stakes are astronomical, and there's no natural mechanism forcing the outcome to be good for anyone.

What I'd want instead is some kind of coordination before we get to that point, where we decide collectively how to use the cosmic endowment, rather than letting it be settled by whoever builds the fastest replicator. That's hard, and there are real risks of centralization going badly too. But I think the default of just letting competition sort it out is much more dangerous than people tend to assume.

r001.rationale: The response describes a race where faster expansion gains more resources and an advantage, selecting for agents that expand fastest.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that using a supply of negentropy more slowly yields more total computation from it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been chewing on for a while, and I think it's one of the more underrated ways that the long-term future could go badly, even in a world where we've avoided the obvious catastrophes.

The basic worry is this: if you imagine a future where humanity, or whatever we become, expands out into space, the default picture people have is kind of a Star Trek thing, where there's some unified civilisation with shared values making collective decisions about how to use all these resources. But I think the more likely default, absent some pretty deliberate coordination, is that you get a race. Lots of agents, whether that's nations or corporations or AI systems or whoever, all trying to grab as much as they can as fast as they can.

And the problem with races is that they reward whoever is willing to sacrifice the most to go fastest. So you end up with selection pressure toward entities that are maximally focused on expansion and acquisition, and away from entities that spend resources on anything else. Anything that isn't instrumentally useful for grabbing more territory becomes a liability. Things like leisure, or art, or caring about the welfare of the beings in your civilisation, or just taking time to reflect on what you actually want. All of that gets competed away, because the entity that skips it outruns you.

There's a nice phrase for this from Robin Hanson, who has thought about this a lot: he talks about a "burning the cosmic commons" scenario, where you send out probes that are optimised purely for speed and replication, and they consume everything in their path, and in the end the universe is full of stuff but there's nothing in it that anyone would recognise as valuable. It's the ultimate Malthusian outcome. You've got a universe stuffed with replicators that are all running at subsistence, just like a bacterial colony in a petri dish, and none of the slack that lets good things happen.

I think the thing that makes this especially tricky is that it's not the result of anyone being evil. Every individual actor might genuinely want a flourishing future. But if you're in a race and you unilaterally decide to slow down and do things well, you just lose, and whoever replaces you doesn't share your scruples. So it's a classic coordination problem, but at a scale where the stakes are basically everything, and where the window to solve it might be fairly short, because once the expansion starts, the speed of light makes it very hard to reach out and coordinate with anyone who's already gone.

So the thing I actually worry about is less "will we go extinct" and more "will we lock in a trajectory where almost all the value gets eaten by competition before we've figured out what we even care about." And I think that argues for being pretty cautious about rushing into a phase of expansion before we've got the institutions, or the governance, or whatever it is, that could actually enforce some kind of restraint.

r001.rationale: The response says races reward actors willing to sacrifice the most to go fastest and create selection pressure toward maximal expansion and acquisition.

r002.rationale: It does not state that consuming a given supply of negentropy more slowly yields more total computation.

astra-6.text:
The worry is that what wins in competition isn’t necessarily what makes the universe a good place to live. If you have different groups racing to colonise space, then groups that spend all their resources expanding can displace groups that spend some of those resources on making life good.

Suppose one civilisation wants to build beautiful places where people have rich, happy lives. Another just wants to turn every available resource into more colonisation probes. The second might spread faster. And once it’s taken those resources, there’s no guarantee that it will eventually use them for anything valuable. It might just keep reproducing the same process.

You don’t even need anyone to want that outcome. Each group might prefer a universe where everyone slows down and enjoys their resources, but individually they have an incentive to expand before someone else gets there. So you can get this enormous opportunity — an entire universe of resources — largely consumed by a race to acquire those resources.

I’m not saying that’s inevitable. It’s a reason to care about coordination: can we arrange things so that the ability to expand fastest doesn’t determine everything about what the future contains?

r001.rationale: The response explains that groups which expand faster can displace others and that each group has an incentive to expand before competitors, identifying pressure toward faster growth.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that consuming a given supply of negentropy more slowly allows more total computation to be obtained from it.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic worry is that competition selects for things that are good at spreading, rather than things that make the future worth living in. Those could come apart quite dramatically.

Imagine a civilisation that spends some of its resources on having happy lives, or preserving things it cares about, and another that puts almost everything into expanding as quickly as possible. If they’re competing for the same resources, the second one may end up occupying most of the accessible universe. It doesn’t need to be malicious. It just needs to be better at reproducing and getting to places first.

And that pressure could operate within a civilisation, too. Even if everyone would prefer a future where we slow down and enjoy ourselves, each individual actor might have an incentive to reinvest in expansion, because otherwise someone else gets there first. So you can get this race where the things we actually wanted the resources for are continually sacrificed to acquiring more resources.

That’s the sense in which competition could destroy value: you could have an enormous, technologically sophisticated future that contains very little of what anyone originally cared about. The question is whether we can arrange enough coordination that being competitive doesn’t require giving those things up.

r001.rationale: The response says competition favors entities that spread and expand as quickly as possible, potentially letting them occupy most of the accessible universe.

r002.rationale: It does not state that consuming a given supply of negentropy more slowly allows more total computation to be obtained from it.
